I	In a stretch of desert north of Cairo, a small fragment of jawbone is forcing a rethink of where
the story of modern apes, including humans, may have begun. The fossil belongs to a newly
identified species, Masripithecus moghraensis, which lived about 17 to 18 million years ago
during the Early Miocene. Described in Science, the fossil was found at Wadi Moghra and is
the first definitive ape from North Africa from this time period — pointing to Egypt, and
possibly the wider North Africa—Middle East region, as a key region in the origin of living
apes, helping fill a gap in the early history of crown Hominoidea, the group that includes all
living apes and their last common ancestor. We spent five years searching for this kind of
fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that
something is missing — and North Africa holds that missing piece.
Until now, Early Miocene sites in North Africa had turned up monkeys, but not apes. That gap
helped shape the view that early apes and their close relatives were restricted to more
southern parts of Africa during this period. Younger ape fossils have been found across Africa,
Asia, and Europe, but their relationships and the group's first emergence remain debated.
Masripithecus shows that apes lived in North Africa during the Early Miocene and that the
species was distinct from similarly aged East African apes, suggesting the fossil record has
been missing part of the record of where the earliest branches of the ape family diversified.
Masripithecus combines Masr, the Arabic word for Egypt, with the Greek word for ape. The
species name, moghraensis, refers to Wadi Moghra, where the remains were recovered in 2023
and 2024.
The fossil consists of a lower jaw, but it preserves a combination of features not seen in any
other known ape from this time. The jaw is robust, with large canine and premolar teeth and
rounded, textured molars. This suggests Masripithecus had a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet,
with the ability to process tougher foods, such as nuts and seeds, when needed. That flexibility
would have been useful in a region becoming more seasonal, where climatic shifts in northern
Africa and Arabia made food supplies less predictable. [Word Count: 377]

Il.	In the library, I watch people navigate information in ways that would have seemed
impossible to previous generations. A research question that once required weeks of archival
work now takes hours. But more than efficiency has changed. The nature of synthesis itself
has transformed. Ideas now move through multiple channels simultaneously. A documentary
provides emotional resonance and visual evidence. Its transcript enables the precision needed
to locate a specific argument. A newsletter unpacks the implications. A podcast allows the
ideas to marinate during a commute. Each mode contributes something the others cannot.
This isn’t decline. It's an expansion.
What strikes me most is the difference between people who've learned to construct what I call
‘containers for attention’ — bounded spaces and practices where different modes of engagement
become possible — and those who haven't. The distinction isn’t about intelligence or discipline.
It’s about environmental architecture. Some people have learned to watch documentaries with
a notebook, listen to podcasts during walks when their minds can wander productively, and
read physical books in deliberately quiet spaces with phones left behind. They're not rejecting
technology. They’re choreographing it.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Others are drowning, attempting sustained thought in environments engineered to prevent it.
They sit with laptops open, seven tabs competing for attention, notifications sliding in from
three different apps, phones vibrating every few minutes. They're trying to read serious
material while fighting a losing battle against behavioural psychology weaponised at scale.

They believe their inability to focus is a personal failure rather than a design problem. They
don’t realise they’re trying to think in a space optimised to prevent thinking. This is where my
understanding of literacy has fundamentally shifted. I used to believe, as I was taught, that
literacy was primarily about decoding text. But watching how people actually learn and think
has convinced me that literacy is about something deeper: the capacity to construct and
navigate environments where understanding becomes possible. [Word Count: 316]

on 18th February, 2026. The inauguration marks a transformative milestone in India’s
administrative governance architecture and reflects the Prime Minister’s commitment to
building a modern, efficient, accessible and citizen-centric governance ecosystem.
For decades, several key government offices and ministries functioned from fragmented and
ageing infrastructure spread across multiple locations. This dispersion led to operational
inefficiencies, coordination challenges, escalating maintenance costs and sub-optimal working
environments. The new building complexes address these issues by consolidating
administrative functions within modern, future-ready facilities. Building complexes feature

digitally integrated offices, structured public interface zones and centralized reception
facilities. These features will foster collaboration, efficiency, seamless governance, improved
citizen engagement and enhanced employee well-being.
The complexes incorporate renewable energy systems, water conservation measures, waste
management solutions and high-performance building envelopes. These measures
significantly reduce environmental impact while enhancing operational efficiency. The
building complexes also include comprehensive safety and security frameworks, such as smart
access control systems, surveillance networks and advanced emergency response
infrastructure, ensuring a secure and accessible environment for officials and visitors. The
Prime Minister reached the Seva Teerth Complex in a motorcade with Union ministers
Manohar Lal and Jitendra Singh and top PMO officials, and inaugurated the complex. The
shift came on a day that marked 95 years since the formal inauguration of New Delhi as
India’s modern capital in 1931. Clad in white and red sandstone, the buildings trace their
referencing material traditions to historic Indian civic and institutional architecture

voting behaviour. The party must also avoid advertising at the cost of the public exchequer or

machinery for campaigning. It should also ensure that public places such as maidans etc., for
holding election meetings, and facilities like the use of helipads are provided to the opposition
parties on the same terms and conditions on which they are used by the party in power. The
issue of advertisement at the cost of public exchequer in the newspapers and other media is
also considered an offence. The ruling government cannot make any ad-hoc appointments in
government, public sector undertakings etc., which may influence the voters.

Asha files an FIR alleging cruelty and dowry harassment against her husband Kunal. The
offence is cognizable and non-bailable, and the local SHO tells Asha that arrest is “mandatory
tonight” because otherwise the police will be blamed. Kunal’s lawyer produces documents
showing he has been cooperating and has a fixed job address. Without collecting any
supporting evidence beyond the complaint, the SHO arrests Kunal immediately. Kunal
challenges the arrest as routine and unjustified.
Which legal position best fits the Arnesh Kumar principle?

options.label: a
options.text:
Arrest is mandatory because cognizable and non-bailable offences require immediate
custody, and necessity inquiry is irrelevant today.

options.label: b
options.text:
Arrest is optional only if complainant withdraws allegations, because police cannot act
without complainant’s continuing consent now.

options.label: c
options.text:
Arrest is not automatic merely because offence is cognizable and non-bailable; power to
arrest differs from justification for arrest.

options.label: d
options.text:
Arrest is lawful only if court issues warrant first, because police cannot arrest without
warrants in cognizable offences ever today.

Ravi is named in an FIR for a workplace scuffle allegedly causing simple injuries, punishable
up to seven years. The Investigating Officer arrests Ravi immediately after the FIR, saying
“registration itself proves a cognizable offence.” No statements are recorded from witnesses,
CCTV is not checked, and medical reports are not collected before arrest. Ravi challenges the
arrest, arguing the officer must first collect evidence and test whether a prima facie cognizable
offence is made out.
What is the strongest view?

options.label: a
options.text:
Arrest valid because a complaint alone is enough to justify arrest, and evidence collection
can happen after custody begins.

options.label: b
options.text:
Arrest invalid because police cannot arrest merely on the basis of complaint/FIR and must
assess necessity under Section 41 CrPC.

options.label: c
options.text:
Arrest valid because offences up to seven years always require immediate arrest, and
Section 41 safeguards apply only above seven years.

options.label: d
options.text:
Arrest invalid only if Magistrate refuses remand later, because police may arrest first and
justify later with reasons afterwards.

Imran is accused of a non-violent offence punishable up to seven years. The IO believes Imran
is involved but does not write any reasons for arrest and does not consider whether arrest is
necessary to prevent tampering, absconding, or further offence. The IO simply states in the
diary: “Arrested as offence is serious.” Imran argues that even if the IO had reason to believe
involvement, arrest still requires recorded reasons showing why arrest is necessary on
statutory grounds.
What is the best legal position?

options.label: a
options.text:
Arrest lawful because seriousness alone satisfies necessity, and recording reasons is
optional when police suspect involvement in offence.

options.label: b
options.text:
Arrest lawful because once reason to believe exists, arrest must follow, and writing reasons
would only delay investigation for police today.

options.label: c
options.text:
Arrest unlawful because for offences up to seven years, arrest needs reason to believe plus
recorded reasons showing why arrest is necessary.

options.label: d
options.text:
Arrest unlawful because police can never arrest in offences up to seven years, and must
always issue summons instead of arresting them.

power to arrest and must only file a chargesheet. The prosecution argues arrest is still
permissible if the accused fails to comply or later compelling reasons arise.
What is the most defensible position?

Arrest illegal because Section 41A notice permanently bars arrest, and police must never
arrest once notice is served.

Arrest legal because person served with Section 41A notice may still be arrested if he fails

XI.	The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 was enacted to ensure that Muslims
in India are governed by Islamic law in personal matters instead of inconsistent regional or
tribal customs. Before 1937, courts often relied on local usage rather than Quranic principles,
which created uncertainty and diluted uniform application of Muslim personal law. In
response to demands from Muslim scholars and leaders, the British Indian legislature passed
this Act, making Shariat the rule of decision in specified matters. The Act was therefore a
major reform measure, as it gave legal recognition to Islamic personal law within the Indian
legal framework and aimed to preserve the religious and cultural identity of Muslims while
replacing contrary customs.
The Act is short but legally important. Section 1 gives its title and extends it to the whole of
India, later fully extended through subsequent amendments. Section 2 is the heart of the Act.
It begins with the overriding phrase “notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary”

XII. Treaties are one of the principal sources of international law and are recognised under Article
88(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice along with custom, general principles,
and judicial decisions and teachings of highly qualified publicists. They are formal written
agreements by which States bind themselves in matters of international responsibility,
cooperation, organisation, trade, security, and rights. The modern law governing treaties is
primarily contained in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969, which came into
force on 27 January 1980. Article 2(1)(a) of the Convention defines a treaty as an international
agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law,
whether contained in one or more related instruments and whatever its designation. The
binding basis of treaty law is the principle of pacta sunt servanda, recognised in Article 26,
which requires every treaty in force to be performed in good faith. Although, as a rule, only
signatory or ratifying States are bound, the North Sea Continental Shelf Cases recognised
that some treaties may have a norm-creating character. States may also enter reservations
under Article 2(1)(d), but reservations cannot defeat the object and purpose of the treaty.
Treaties may broadly be classified as law-making treaties and contractual treaties. Law-
making treaties are generally multilateral and create general binding norms, often in fields
such as human rights, maritime law, international mandates, tribunals, and waterways. They
resemble legislation and impose duties independent of private bargains. Contractual treaties,
on the other hand, are usually bilateral or limited in scope, and are based on mutual benefit,
such as trade, alliance, or conveyance agreements. The Vienna Convention governs the
making of treaties through stages such as adoption, authentication, expression of consent,
ratification, accession, and reservations. Ratification reflects approval, while accession refers
to becoming a party after the minimum ratification requirement has been met. Under Articles
34 to 37, third States are generally neither bound nor benefited by a treaty without their
consent, though customary international law may eventually make some treaty rules binding
more broadly.
The Convention also regulates invalidity, suspension, and termination. Under Articles 46 to
58, a treaty may be invalidated for conflict with domestic law regarding competence, error,
fraud, corruption, coercion, or conflict with jus cogens, that is, peremptory norms such as
genocide, piracy, apartheid, or torture. A treaty may terminate by withdrawal, breach,
impossibility of performance, conclusion of a later treaty on the same subject, fundamental
change of circumstances, or emergence of a new jus cogens norm. Thus, treaties remain a
central instrument of international law because they create legal certainty, regulate inter-
State conduct, and promote peace, order, and cooperation in the international system. [Word
Count: 434]

XIV. The ongoing Sabarimala reference before a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court has revived
a foundational constitutional debate on the relationship between Articles 25 and 26 and the
continued validity of the Essential Religious Practice (ERP) test. The ERP test emerged from
an obiter observation in Durgah Committee v. Syed Hussain Ali (1961), where the Court
stated that only those practices which are “essential and integral” to a religion deserve
protection under Article 26. This modified the earlier approach in Shirur Mutt (1954), where
the Court had principally distinguished between secular practices, which can be regulated,
and religious practices, which receive constitutional protection. The present reference
therefore raises a central issue: whether courts should continue identifying essential religious
practices, or whether the inquiry should only be whether a practice is religious or secular.
During the hearing, Justice BV Nagarathna suggested that once a practice is determined to be
strictly secular, everything else would fall within the religious sphere, making the ERP test
unnecessary. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, however, noted that even such a distinction
would still require the Court to evolve standards for deciding what counts as religious and
what counts as secular, thereby bringing the inquiry back to the same constitutional problem.
Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan argued that the ERP test should be abandoned
because Articles 25 and 26 themselves are clear, and that religious affairs should be
understood through the constitutional text rather than broad judicial labels. In his
submission, Article 25(1), which is expressly made “subject to the other provisions” of Part III,
should be read as subject mainly to horizontal equality provisions such as Articles 15(2), 17,
23, and 24, whereas Article 26 stands on a stronger footing because it does not contain the
same phrase.
A major interpretive issue is whether Article 26(b), which protects a denomination’s right to
manage its own affairs in matters of religion, is subject to Article 25(2)(b), which permits the
State to enact laws for social reform and temple entry for all classes and sections of Hindus.

throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of
Hindus. Article 26(b) protects a denomination’s right to manage its own affairs in matters of
religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Sai Deepak argued that Article 26 is not
controlled by Article 25(2), and that denominational rights were deliberately insulated from
broader constitutional limitations. In contrast, Senior Advocate Gopal Subramanium argued
that Article 26 must be harmonised with Article 25(2)(a) and (b), so that denominational
temples may still be subject to reform laws opening access to excluded classes. Thus, the
reference now squarely presents two major constitutional questions: whether the ERP doctrine
should survive, and how individual religious freedom under Article 25 must be reconciled with
collective denominational autonomy under Article 26. [Word Count: 484]

questions.stimulus:
XVI. The recent announcement by Air India, hinting at possible pay cuts or even de-rostering for
crew members with a higher Body Mass Index (BMI), may, at first glance, appear to be a
prudent and well-intentioned step toward ensuring fitness and operational safety. Aviation,
after all, is a profession where physical readiness is essential. Yet, the timing of this decision
—coinciding with the week an anti-obesity drug, semaglutide, went off patent and nearly 40
products entered the Indian market— signals something deeper.
India today faces a mounting burden of obesity and associated metabolic conditions such as
diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver disease, and dyslipidaemia. Nearly a quarter of Indians are
overweight or obese. One in 10 adults live with diabetes, one in three with hypertension, and a
substantial proportion has fatty liver disease. Even more concerning is the rapid rise of obesity
among children. The causes, which are neither obscure nor debated, include the proliferation
of ultra-processed or high fat, salt and sugar-content foods, and increasingly sedentary
lifestyles shaped by urban work patterns, shrinking open spaces, chronic stress, alcohol
consumption, and inadequate sleep. Compounding this is a genetic predisposition among
Indians and South Asians toward excess body fat despite a seemingly lean appearance — the
so-called “thin-fat” phenotype.
Historically, in a society long shaped by undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies, excess
weight was once perceived as a marker of prosperity. Consequently, as overweight and obesity
began rising over the past two decades, public discourse remained muted, almost reluctant to
confront this emerging reality. Then came the pharmaceutical response. Around this time last
year, another anti-obesity drug, tirzepatide, entered the Indian market and rapidly became
one of its highest-selling medications. Its commercial success revealed not just clinical demand
but also the emergence of a vast and lucrative therapeutic marketplace. With semaglutide now
available at a remarkably lower cost, the market potential has expanded further.
Over the past year, however, a more troubling pattern has emerged. Prescription medicines
cannot be directly advertised to the public, yet pharmaceutical companies have grown adept at
navigating these constraints. Surrogate advertising — often framed as public awareness
campaigns — has become increasingly sophisticated. In the past year, the country witnessed
full page newspaper campaigns, and billboards at major urban areas regarding obesity;
influencer endorsements for medical products; and sponsored features that resemble
independent journalism, subtly shaping public perception without explicitly naming the drugs.
The messaging on drugs from pharmaceuticals is rarely overt; instead, it is nuanced,
persistent, and highly effective, gradually reshaping both public expectations and clinical
practice. In such an environment, the boundary between genuine scientific advancement and
commercial enthusiasm begins to blur. New drugs are presented as_ transformative
breakthroughs, while their uncertainties receive far less attention. [Word Count: 446]

XVII. India’s cloud is not only virtual — it is increasingly physical, resource-intensive and expanding
at an extraordinary pace. As digital adoption deepens, artificial intelligence scales, and
businesses shift relentlessly to cloud-based operations, the country is experiencing a wave of
hyperscale and colocation data-centre construction unlike anything seen before. These
facilities have quietly become the invisible scaffolding of India’s digital economy, powering
everything from payments and logistics to e-governance, entertainment, healthcare, and an
emerging AI industry. They bring investment, jobs, efficiency, and the promise of a
technologically-advanced future.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Yet, beneath this progress lies an uncomfortable truth: data centres are energy-hungry and
water-thirsty, and their rapid growth risks creating a severe environmental and hydrological
burden that India is not prepared to handle. The scale of expansion explains the growing
alarm. India’s data-centre capacity has surged in recent years, and analysts forecast that it
may multiply several-fold by the end of this decade as AI computing, 5G applications and
cloud services proliferate. Each additional megawatt of computing load generates enormous
heat that must be dissipated constantly, every hour of every day.
To manage this heat, most large centres rely heavily on water-intensive cooling techniques
such as evaporative cooling towers. Independent studies estimate that if this expansion
continues unchecked, India’s data-centre sector could collectively withdraw hundreds of
billions of litres of water annually within a few years. These numbers are not abstractions.

Data centres are concentrated in coastal and metropolitan hubs like Mumbai, Chennai,
Hyderabad, Bengaluru and the National Capital Region — precisely those regions that
already face severe water scarcity during peak summers, chronic groundwater depletion, and
frequent competition between residential demand, agriculture, and industrial use. The
creation of sprawling digital infrastructures that depend on constant water supply in water-
stressed basins poses a clear and imminent risk.
The question then arises: why do data centres require so much water in the first place? The
answer lies in basic physics and economics. High-density servers, especially those supporting
GPU-heavy AI workloads, generate intense heat. Water-cooled evaporative towers remain the
industry's preferred solution because they are efficient and cost-effective at scale. A single
hyperscale data centre can require millions of litres of water per day at peak operational loads.
Beyond direct consumption, the indirect water footprint is equally significant: electricity
generation from thermal power plants, manufacturing of servers and components,
construction of massive concrete-and-steel facilities, and water treatment processes all
contribute to the sector’s overall hydrological impact. [Word Count: 400]
